title: Macroscopic hematuria caused by running-induced traumatic bladder mucosal contusions
claims: Twelve patients visited an outpatient clinic with asymptomatic macroscopic haematuria after running as the chief complaint between January 2014 and December 2017.
In 9 of 12 patients (75%), cystoscopy showed erythematous and/or hyperemic mucosal contusions at the centre of the posterior bladder wall, the same site in all patients.
The authors attributed the contusion to repeated contact of the posterior bladder wall against the fixed bladder neck by vertical motion in the empty bladder lumen during running.
All patients with bladder contusion were male, with a median age of 48 (range 40–66) years, and had run distances over 10 km.

Gross haematuria resolved within a few days without treatment after running cessation; follow-up cystoscopy in four patients showed resolution within a few months, and five patients relapsed after restarting running.
Three of the 12 patients (25%) had another significant urological disease: non-muscle-invasive bladder tumour, lower ureteral tumour, and impacted lower ureteral stone.
The article cites a prevalence of running-induced haematuria of about 20–25%, and reports that macroscopic haematuria is rarer, with about 2% prevalence in marathon runners.
The authors recommend urological evaluation including cytology and CT in addition to cystoscopy for running-induced gross haematuria.
